subject: Porte et al. (1980)
object: Porte et al. (1980) described 3 brothers with progressive myocardial deficiency. On histology, most cardiac muscle cells showed massive storage of PAS-negative proteinaceous material. Electron microscopy showed that this material consisted of sinuous filaments 7 to 10 nm in diameter, similar to intermediate filaments. Filament storage coincided with disintegration of neighbouring myofibrils. Z-band changes gave rise to rod-like bodies, and Z-band material associated with sarcoplasmic reticulum tubules formed more complex structures.

subject: Porte et al. (1980)
object: Porte et al. (1980) found that, in the 3 brothers, filament storage and myofibrillar disintegration always occurred in areas of extensive development and involution of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, together with relatively high glycogen accumulation. A few skeletal muscle fibers also showed discrete sarcoplasmic reticulum proliferation, glycogen overload and filament deposits.

subject: Porte et al. (1980)
object: Porte et al. (1980) suggested that a disturbance in the metabolism of desmin might be involved in this cardiomyopathy. They described desmin as the protein subunit of intermediate filaments and a fundamental component of Z bands. Because of the marked sarcoplasmic reticulum abnormalities, they also suggested that a chronic defect in calcium regulation might play a role.

subject: Stoeckel et al. (1981)
object: Stoeckel et al. (1981) described an unusual familial cardiomyopathy characterized by aberrant accumulations of desmin-type intermediate filaments.

subject: Wolburg et al. (1982)
object: Wolburg et al. (1982) reported 2 unrelated 32-year-old patients with a congenital, slowly progressive skeletal myopathy. One patient (case 2) also had congenital paresis of the pupillary dilator muscle and cardiomyopathy. The course ended in severe impairment of skeletal muscle function in case 1 but not in case 2.

subject: Wolburg et al. (1982)
object: In both patients, Wolburg et al. (1982) found abnormal variation in muscle fiber caliber on muscle biopsy, and in case 1 atrophic fibers were grouped in places. Inclusions with dense granular and fine filamentous components, consistent with cytoplasmic bodies, were present in about one-third of fibers in case 1 and about one-tenth in case 2. The biopsies also showed Z-disk streaming or disintegration and subsarcolemmal pure filamentous bodies.

subject: Wolburg et al. (1982)
object: Wolburg et al. (1982) proposed that the disorder is caused by a basic defect in myofilament biosynthesis. They suggested that this defect is presumably triggered by a neurogenic factor that affects the trophic influence of the neuron on the muscle cell.

subject: Chapon et al. (1989)
object: Chapon et al. (1989) described 3 patients from 3 successive generations of a family who had cytoplasmic body myopathy and presented with respiratory insufficiency. The patients were 72, 45, and 18 years old. Clinical onset was at about 40 years of age in the 2 older patients and at 18 years in the youngest. Serum muscle enzymes and leukocyte maltase activity were normal. Muscle biopsy in all 3 patients showed numerous cytoplasmic (spheroid) bodies within type I muscle fibers.

subject: Chapon et al. (1989)
object: Chapon et al. (1989) reported cytoplasmic body myopathy in 3 successive generations of 1 family. They noted that cytoplasmic body myopathy occurring in families has rarely been reported, and that presentation with respiratory insufficiency in adult life is even rarer.

subject: Abe et al. (1993)
object: Abe et al. (1993) described a Japanese kindred with autosomal dominant progressive myopathy with diffuse cytoplasmic bodies, in which 12 patients across 4 successive generations had weakness and atrophy of muscles of the distal extremities, neck, thorax, and shoulder girdles. Mean age at onset was 42 years, and patients became disabled after 5 to 10 years due to chronic respiratory failure. Serum creatine kinase was normal or slightly elevated, and EMG showed predominantly myopathic changes with slight neurogenic change. Males were more frequently affected than females (2:1).

subject: Abe et al. (1993)
object: Abe et al. (1993) reported that autopsy of 2 affected members of the kindred revealed numerous cytoplasmic bodies in skeletal muscle, predominantly in type I fibers, with smooth and cardiac muscle also affected. Electron microscopy showed dense central cores of myofilaments surrounded by radiating filaments.

subject: Abe et al. (1993)
object: Abe et al. (1993) observed autosomal dominant inheritance of cytoplasmic body myopathy through 4 successive generations of a Japanese kindred.

subject: Vajsar et al. (1993)
object: Vajsar et al. (1993) reported 2 sibs who developed cardiomyopathy several years before the onset of slowly progressive muscle weakness. The authors concluded that these clinical and pathologic features characterized a rare familial myopathy associated with an unusual distribution of desmin intermediate filament proteins in skeletal and probably also cardiac muscle.

subject: Vajsar et al. (1993)
object: In the 2 sibs, Vajsar et al. (1993) found subsarcolemmal crescents of dark eosinophilic material in both type I and type II fibers on skeletal muscle biopsy. This material stained for desmin and ubiquitin but for no other cytoskeletal proteins. On electron microscopy, the deposits were aggregates of granular and filamentous material arising from Z-bands. Follow-up biopsies 6 years later showed more fibers containing desmin- and ubiquitin-positive subsarcolemmal aggregates.

subject: Horowitz and Schmalbruch (1994)
object: Horowitz and Schmalbruch (1994) described a large kindred with autosomal dominant distal myopathy. Onset was in early to middle adulthood with gait disturbance due to distal leg weakness. Over 5 to 10 years the disease progressed to involve all extremities and the bulbar, respiratory and facial muscles. Cardiac involvement was frequent, with arrhythmias, conduction blocks and congestive heart failure, and led to premature death.

subject: Horowitz and Schmalbruch (1994)
object: In the family reported by Horowitz and Schmalbruch (1994), electromyography showed prominent spontaneous activity, short-duration motor unit potentials and polyphasia. Muscle biopsies from several family members at different stages of the disease showed desmin storage and autophagocytosis. The authors noted that this distal myopathy differed from other phenotypically similar disorders in its rapid progression, fatal course and pathologic features.

subject: Goebel (1995)
object: In a review, Goebel (1995) stated that desmin pathology in human neuromuscular disorders always takes the form of increased amounts of desmin, either diffuse or focal. Focal accumulation occurs in two forms: with certain inclusion bodies (cytoplasmic and spheroid bodies), and as patchier granulofilamentous material. Both lesions had been found in certain families affected by a myopathy and/or cardiomyopathy. Other proteins, such as dystrophin, vimentin, actin, ubiquitin, and alpha-B crystallin, may also be overexpressed.

subject: Goebel (1995)
object: Goebel (1995) suggested that desmin pathology may be genetically regulated, or may simply reflect severely impaired metabolism of several proteins within muscle fibers.

subject: Ariza et al. (1995)
object: Ariza et al. (1995) described a 28-year-old man with desmin myopathy who had generalized muscular atrophy, cardiomyopathy, and intestinal malabsorption and pseudo-obstruction. The authors stated that this was the first report of intestinal smooth muscle involvement in desmin myopathy, in addition to its known skeletal and cardiac muscle features.

subject: Ariza et al. (1995)
object: In the patient described by Ariza et al. (1995), pathologic study found abundant granular and filamentous aggregates in the sarcoplasm that stained strongly for desmin. These aggregates were present throughout the skeletal muscle, the myocardium, and the smooth muscle of the intestine. On electron microscopy, the aggregates were continuous with Z lines or dense bodies. The authors also found axonal spheroids that stained for neurofilament in the spinal cord and roots, which they called an extremely rare combination of intermediate filament pathology in the neuromuscular system.

subject: Messina et al. (1997)
object: Messina et al. (1997) characterized an autosomal dominant disorder involving dilated cardiomyopathy, cardiac conduction-system disease, and adult-onset limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, which they called FDC-CDM (familial dilated cardiomyopathy, conduction disease, and myopathy).

subject: Messina et al. (1997)
object: By genomewide scan, Messina et al. (1997) identified a region on chromosome 6q significantly linked to the myopathy in FDC-CDM (maximum lod score 4.99 at theta = 0.00 for D6S262). Haplotype analysis refined the interval to 3 cM between D6S1705 and D6S1656, excluding striated muscle-expressed genes in the region including laminin alpha-2, laminin alpha-4, triadin, and phospholamban.

subject: Messina et al. (1997)
object: Messina et al. (1997) used linkage to exclude genomic regions known to be linked to dilated cardiomyopathy and muscular dystrophy phenotypes, confirming genetic heterogeneity and identifying FDC-CDM as genetically distinct.

subject: Goldfarb et al. (1998)
object: Goldfarb et al. (1998) described desmin-related myopathy as a familial disorder characterized by skeletal muscle weakness associated with cardiac conduction blocks, arrhythmias, and restrictive heart failure, and by intracytoplasmic accumulation of desmin-reactive deposits in cardiac and skeletal muscle cells.

subject: Goldfarb et al. (1998)
object: Goldfarb et al. (1998) noted that involvement of the desmin gene (DES) had been excluded in 3 families diagnosed with desmin-related myopathy.

subject: Goldfarb et al. (1998)
object: Goldfarb et al. (1998) reported 2 families with desmin-related cardioskeletal myopathy: one with adult-onset skeletal myopathy and mild cardiac involvement, and a second characterized by a childhood-onset aggressive course of cardiac and skeletal myopathy.

subject: Goldfarb et al. (1998)
object: In a family with adult-onset skeletal myopathy and mild cardiac involvement, Goldfarb et al. (1998) identified a heterozygous A337P mutation in the highly conserved carboxy-terminal end of the desmin rod domain.

subject: Goldfarb et al. (1998)
object: In a family with childhood-onset aggressive cardiac and skeletal myopathy, Goldfarb et al. (1998) detected compound heterozygosity for 2 DES mutations, A360P and N393I, in the carboxy-terminal end of the desmin rod domain.

subject: Muñoz-Mármol et al. (1998)
object: Muñoz-Mármol et al. (1998) reported a patient with severe generalized myopathy. The patient's muscle showed abnormal accumulation of desmin intermediate filaments within the sarcoplasm.

subject: Muñoz-Mármol et al. (1998)
object: In muscle tissue from a patient with severe generalized myopathy, Muñoz-Mármol et al. (1998) found a DES mutation encoding a 7-amino acid deletion within the coiled-coil segment of desmin. The wildtype desmin allele was absent from the patient's muscle. Recombinant desmin carrying this deletion did not form proper desmin intermediate filament networks in cultured cells and did not assemble into 10-nm filaments in vitro.

subject: DES 7-aa deletion within the coiled-coil segment
Muñoz-Mármol et al. (1998)
object: Muñoz-Mármol et al. (1998) concluded that their findings were direct evidence that a desmin mutation can cause human myopathy. They noted that desmin-null mice form muscle fibers with Z disks and normal sarcomeres, but these muscles are mechanically fragile and degenerate with repeated contraction.

subject: Sjöberg et al. (1999)
object: Sjöberg et al. (1999) studied a large 6-generation Ashkenazi Jewish family with autosomal dominant desmin-related myopathy of distal onset.

subject: Sjöberg et al. (1999)
object: In affected members of a large 6-generation Ashkenazi Jewish family with autosomal dominant distal desmin-related myopathy, Sjöberg et al. (1999) identified a heterozygous L345P missense mutation in the DES gene that cosegregated with the disease; it was the first point mutation in desmin reported to cosegregate with autosomal dominant desmin-related myopathy. The mutation lies at an evolutionarily highly conserved position of the coiled-coil rod domain important for dimer formation.

subject: Sjöberg et al. (1999)
object: Sjöberg et al. (1999) found that L345P desmin was incapable of forming filamentous networks in transfected HeLa and SW13 cells, and concluded that the mutation causes myopathy by interfering in a dominant-negative manner with the dimerization-polymerization process of intermediate filament assembly.

subject: Melberg et al. (1999)
object: Melberg et al. (1999) studied a Swedish family with myopathy and cardiomyopathy. They investigated 21 family members neurologically and cardiologically and reviewed the charts of 2 deceased affected patients. Twelve patients had myopathy. Weakness was axial in mildly affected patients, axial and predominantly distal in moderately affected patients, and generalized in severely affected patients. Electromyography showed myopathic signs in 10 patients.

subject: Melberg et al. (1999)
object: In this Swedish family, Melberg et al. (1999) found that muscle biopsies showed myopathic changes, rimmed vacuoles, and accumulation of desmin, dystrophin, and other proteins. Electron microscopy showed granulofilamentous changes and disorganized myofibrils.

subject: Melberg et al. (1999)
object: Melberg et al. (1999) reported that several members of the family had episodes of chest pain or palpitations. Three men had arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, with documented nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, atrial flutter, and ventricular dilatation affecting mainly the right ventricle. Two of the 3 men received pacemakers for atrioventricular block and sick sinus syndrome.

subject: Melberg et al. (1999)
object: Melberg et al. (1999) concluded that the disorder in this Swedish family was inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, with variable onset and severity of both skeletal muscle and cardiac involvement.

subject: Melberg et al. (1999)
object: Melberg et al. (1999) performed linkage analysis of candidate chromosomal regions in this Swedish family. They found a maximum 2-point LOD score of 2.76 at marker D10S1752 on 10q and a multipoint peak LOD score of 3.06 between markers D10S605 and D10S215. They suggested that 10q22.3 may harbor the genetic defect for myofibrillar myopathy with ARVC.

subject: Saavedra-Matiz et al. (2000)
object: Saavedra-Matiz et al. (2000) studied a large family with an autosomal dominant hereditary distal myopathy. The myopathy progressed slowly, began in early adulthood in the distal leg muscles, and caused a gait disturbance. Most affected family members also had cardiomyopathy, presenting as conduction block or congestive heart failure. On histology, desmin had accumulated in the subsarcolemmal spaces of myofibers.

subject: Saavedra-Matiz et al. (2000)
object: In this large family, Saavedra-Matiz et al. (2000) used linkage analysis to map the disease gene to chromosome 2q33. The gene lay within a 17-cM segment bounded by the markers D2S2248 and D2S401. The authors considered desmin the best candidate gene.

subject: Park et al. (2000)
object: Park et al. (2000) identified a heterozygous de novo A-to-G change at the +3 position of the intron 3 splice donor site of the DES gene (IVS3+3A-G) in a patient with sporadic skeletal and cardiac myopathy. They found it by sequencing cDNA and genomic DNA. When they expressed genomic DNA fragments carrying the mutation, the result was deletion of exon 3.

subject: Park et al. (2000)
object: Park et al. (2000) identified a G-to-A transition at the -1 position of the intron 2 splice acceptor site of the DES gene (IVS2-1G-A) in a second, unrelated patient with a similar skeletal and cardiac myopathy. When they expressed genomic DNA fragments carrying the mutation, the result was deletion of exon 3.

subject: Park et al. (2000)
object: Park et al. (2000) found that both splice mutations caused skipping of exon 3, giving an in-frame deletion of 32 codons. They predicted that the mutant desmin would lack 32 amino acids from the 1B segment of the alpha-helical rod. When the mutant desmin was expressed in vimentin-deficient SW13 cells, abnormal coarse clumps of desmin-positive material aggregated throughout the cytoplasm.

subject: Park et al. (2000)
object: Park et al. (2000) described desmin myopathy as a hereditary or sporadic cardiac and skeletal myopathy characterized by desmin-reactive deposits that accumulate inside the cytoplasm of muscle cells.

subject: Kaminska et al. (2004)
object: Kaminska et al. (2004) studied 3 families with skeletal or cardioskeletal myopathy caused by small in-frame deletions in the desmin gene. They described desminopathy as a disease characterized by progressive limb muscle weakness and by desmin-reactive granular aggregates that accumulate in the myofibers.

subject: Kaminska et al. (2004)
object: In patients with desmin-related myopathy, Kaminska et al. (2004) identified a new in-frame deletion in the DES gene, E359_S361del. It changes the heptad periodicity of the 2B coiled-coil segment. Structural analysis showed that the deletion adds a second stutter immediately downstream of the naturally occurring stutter, which doubles the extent of local coiled-coil unwinding. In expression studies in 2 cell lines, the mutant desmin could not polymerize into a functional filamentous network.

subject: Kaminska et al. (2004)
object: In patients with desmin-related myopathy, Kaminska et al. (2004) identified a new in-frame deletion in the DES gene, N366del. It changes the heptad periodicity of the 2B coiled-coil segment and turns the wild-type stutter into a stammer, which the authors expected to cause extra overwinding of the coiled coil. In expression studies in 2 cell lines, the mutant desmin could not polymerize into a functional filamentous network.

subject: Kaminska et al. (2004)
object: Kaminska et al. (2004) concluded that small in-frame deletions in the 2B coiled-coil segment of desmin change the coiled-coil geometry in specific ways. They proposed that this causes fatal damage to desmin filament assembly, leading to breakdown of muscle cells and to skeletal or cardioskeletal myopathy.

subject: Selcen et al. (2004)
object: Selcen et al. (2004) reviewed 63 unrelated patients diagnosed with myofibrillar myopathy at the Mayo Clinic between 1977 and 2003. Mean age at onset was 54 +/- 16 years. Weakness was both proximal and distal in 77% of patients and proximal only in 13%, and cardiomyopathy was diagnosed in 16%. EMG showed a myopathic pattern with abnormal electrical irritability. Thirteen patients had abnormal nerve conduction studies, but 4 of these had long-standing diabetes.

subject: Selcen et al. (2004)
object: In the 63 patients studied by Selcen et al. (2004), trichrome-stained sections showed abnormal muscle fibers containing amorphous, granular or pleomorphic hyaline structures, which were strongly congophilic, as well as vacuoles containing membranous material. Electron microscopy showed progressive myofibrillar degeneration beginning at the Z-disk, accumulation of degraded filamentous material, and dislocated membranous organelles trapped in autophagic vacuoles.

subject: Selcen et al. (2004)
object: Selcen et al. (2004) used semiquantitative immunostaining and found that, on average, 90% of abnormal fibers abnormally expressed myotilin, 75% desmin, 75% alpha-B-crystallin, 70% dystrophin and 70% beta-amyloid precursor protein. They concluded that immunostains for these proteins, especially myotilin, are useful adjuncts in diagnosing MFM.

subject: Selcen et al. (2004)
object: Selcen et al. (2004) screened 63 unrelated patients with MFM for mutations in desmin, alpha-B-crystallin, telethonin and syncoilin. Four patients carried missense mutations in the head or tail region of desmin (DES), and 2 carried truncating mutations in the C-terminal domain of alpha-B-crystallin (CRYAB). No patient had a mutation in syncoilin or telethonin.

subject: Selcen et al. (2004)
object: Only 6 of 63 MFM patients had mutations in desmin or alpha-B-crystallin. Selcen et al. (2004) therefore concluded that MFM is morphologically distinct but genetically heterogeneous.

subject: Ferreiro et al. (2004)
object: Ferreiro et al. (2004) noted that desmin-related myopathies (DRMs) are a heterogeneous group of muscle disorders defined by intrasarcoplasmic desmin aggregates, and that mutations in the desmin and alpha-B crystallin genes account for approximately one-third of DRM cases.

subject: Ferreiro et al. (2004)
object: Ferreiro et al. (2004) found that, in the original German family with early-onset recessive desmin-related myopathy with Mallory body-like inclusions (MB-DRM), the disease was linked to the SEPN1 locus on 1p36. Affected patients had a homozygous 92-nucleotide SEPN1 deletion (del 92 nucleotide -19/+73). The authors reported that MB-DRM shares identical clinical features with SEPN-related myopathy and proposed that it be classified as SEPN-related myopathy. They said these findings substantiated the molecular heterogeneity of DRM.

subject: Shelton et al. (2004)
object: Shelton et al. (2004) described a 1-year-old male neutered Australian Shepherd dog with chronic lameness, contractures, and exercise intolerance. The dog had elevated serum creatine kinase, complex repetitive discharges on electromyography, and clinically identified cardiomyopathy. Light and electron microscopy and immunohistochemistry of muscle biopsies showed a myofibrillar myopathy with accumulation of desmin and other proteins. The authors stated that this was the first report of myofibrillar myopathy in the dog.

subject: Bär et al. (2007)
object: Bär et al. (2007) reported 3 novel mutations in the non-alpha-helical carboxy-terminal tail domain of desmin (DES) in patients with desmin-related myofibrillar myopathy: c.1325C>T (p.T442I), c.1360C>T (p.R454W), and c.1379G>T (p.S460I).

subject: Bär et al. (2007)
object: Bär et al. (2007) studied the 3 novel tail mutations and 4 previously described ones (E413K, K449T, I451M, V469M) using in vitro filament assembly and transfected C2C12 myoblasts. All mutants except E413K and R454W assembled into intermediate filaments in vitro, and all except E413K were incorporated into filament arrays in cells. However, viscometric assays showed that filament properties differed significantly from wild-type desmin. When the mutants were coassembled with wild-type desmin, filament formation and filament-filament interactions were severely disturbed, which the authors interpreted as an inherent incompatibility of mutant and wild-type protein.

subject: Bär et al. (2007)
object: Bär et al. (2007) suggested that the various clinical phenotypes caused by desmin tail mutations may reflect altered interactions of the tail domain with different components of the myoblast cytoskeleton. They proposed that this may lead to diminished biomechanical properties and/or altered metabolism of the individual myocyte.

subject: Bergman et al. (2007)
object: Bergman et al. (2007) reported 2 distantly related Dutch families with autosomal dominant desmin-related myopathy affecting 15 family members. The clinical picture was highly heterogeneous, ranging from isolated dilated cardiomyopathy to a more generalized skeletal myopathy with mild respiratory problems. Muscle biopsies showed intracytoplasmic desmin aggregates on desmin and p62 staining.

subject: Bergman et al. (2007)
object: In affected members of 2 distantly related Dutch families with desmin-related myopathy, Bergman et al. (2007) identified a novel heterozygous missense mutation, S13F, in the head domain of the desmin gene (DES) that cosegregated with the disease phenotype.

subject: Bergman et al. (2007)
object: Bergman et al. (2007) stressed the importance of analyzing the desmin gene in patients with familial cardiac conduction disease, dilated cardiomyopathy, and/or progressive skeletal myopathy resembling limb-girdle muscular dystrophy.

subject: Pica et al. (2008)
object: Pica et al. (2008) described a Chinese man with desmin myopathy, complete heart block, and mild weakness of the proximal and distal limbs. Family members who carried the mutation had a similar or milder phenotype.

subject: Pica et al. (2008)
object: Pica et al. (2008) found a novel heterozygous missense mutation, S13F, in the desmin gene in a Chinese man with desmin myopathy and complete heart block. Family members carrying the mutation also had the disorder. The mutation lies at a protein kinase C phosphorylation site within a highly conserved nonapeptide sequence in the head domain of desmin. When the mutant desmin cDNA was expressed in cell lines, it induced large desmin accumulations while a filamentous network was preserved.

subject: Kuhl et al. (2008)
object: In a follow-up study of the Swedish family with autosomal dominant myofibrillar myopathy and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC7), which had previously been tentatively mapped to a 10.6-Mb region on 10q22.3 between D10S605 and D10S215, Kuhl et al. (2008) re-examined the linkage with a high-density SNP panel (Affymetrix Human Mapping 10K Array) and confirmed it. They found no other region with significant evidence for linkage and narrowed the critical interval to 4.27 Mb between D10S1645 and D10S1786.

subject: Kuhl et al. (2008)
object: Kuhl et al. (2008) found that the narrowed region contained 18 candidate genes, 17 of which (RAI17, PPIF, C10ORF56, SFTPA1, SFTPA2, SFTPA1B, SFTPA2B, SFTPD, C10ORF57, PLAC9, ANXA11, MAT1A, DYDC1, DYDC2, C10ORF58, TSPAN14, and SH2D4B) are shared with the CMD1C region. They found no disease-causing mutation in the coding regions of these genes. Sequence analysis also excluded metavinculin (VCL) and ZASP/cypher (LDB3), which lie proximal and distal to the linked region.

subject: Kuhl et al. (2008)
object: To search for submicroscopic and intragenic deletions by PCR, Kuhl et al. (2008) generated hybrid cell lines carrying only the affected or only the normal chromosome 10 homolog. All sequence-tagged sites and exons were present on both homologs. The authors speculated that regulatory mutations in 1 of the 18 genes from 10q22.3 cause a heterogeneous spectrum of clinically distinct myodegenerative disorders that affect skeletal and cardiac muscle to variable degrees.

subject: Piñol-Ripoll et al. (2009)
object: Piñol-Ripoll et al. (2009) reported a girl, the only child of consanguineous (uncle-niece) parents, with recurrent syncope from age 6 months, initially attributed to an accessory conduction pathway/Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, followed by progressive syncopal, presyncopal and cyanotic attacks from age 3 years. At age 15 she had a long narrow face, bilateral facial weakness, ptosis, symmetric scapular winging, atrophy of masseter, temporalis, sternocleidomastoid and trunk muscles, pes cavus, mild shoulder girdle and distal limb weakness, hypoactive reflexes, and 2-fold elevated creatine kinase; EMG showed complex repetitive discharges, some myotonic discharges and a myopathic pattern.

subject: Piñol-Ripoll et al. (2009)
object: Piñol-Ripoll et al. (2009) found on Holter monitoring of their patient monomorphic and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, QT prolongation and second-degree AV block, requiring an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator and pacemaker; at 18 years she had recurrent ventricular tachyarrhythmias, mild left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVEF 45%), right ventricular dilatation, markedly enlarged atria and restrictive cardiomyopathy. Skeletal weakness progressed rapidly, diarrhea, vomiting and weight loss suggested smooth intestinal muscle involvement, and she died of cardiac failure before age 21.

subject: Piñol-Ripoll et al. (2009)
object: Piñol-Ripoll et al. (2009) found on deltoid muscle biopsy variation in fiber size and, in more than 90% of fibers, peripheral deposits of homogeneous eosinophilic material that were Congo red positive and strongly desmin-immunoreactive, along with some rimmed vacuoles; electron microscopy showed granulofilamentous material, consistent with myofibrillar myopathy. The inclusions differed from the amorphous patches seen in most patients with dominant or de novo desmin mutations.

subject: Piñol-Ripoll et al. (2009)
object: In the patient with infantile-onset cardiomyopathy and myofibrillar myopathy, Piñol-Ripoll et al. (2009) identified a homozygous 21-nucleotide deletion in the DES gene, predicting in-frame loss of 7 amino acids (RARVDVE; p.R173_E179del) in the 1B helix domain, removing a full heptad. Both consanguineous parents were heterozygous and unaffected. The mutation was noted to prevent desmin filament assembly in transfected MCF-7 cells; the same homozygous deletion had previously been reported by Muñoz-Mármol et al. in a severely affected boy.

subject: Piñol-Ripoll et al. (2009)
object: Piñol-Ripoll et al. (2009) stated that their case was the first exhaustively proven autosomal recessive desminopathy, as heterozygous carrier parents were unaffected; they noted that about 6% of desminopathy patients show autosomal recessive inheritance with childhood onset (average 5 years).

subject: Piñol-Ripoll et al. (2009)
object: Piñol-Ripoll et al. (2009) concluded that patients with desmin-related cardiomyopathy are at high risk of ventricular arrhythmia and should be considered for implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement even before ventricular dysfunction becomes evident.

subject: van Tintelen et al. (2009)
object: van Tintelen et al. (2009) studied 27 carriers or obligate carriers of a DES p.S13F founder mutation from 5 families, who showed a fully penetrant yet variable phenotype. All patients had cardiac involvement characterized by high-grade AV block at young ages and important right ventricular involvement: right bundle branch block in 10 patients (sometimes as the first manifestation) and right ventricular heart failure in 6, including 2 who fulfilled diagnostic criteria for arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. The authors concluded that the phenotype was predominantly cardiologic, with early conduction disease, right bundle branch block and/or right ventricular tachycardias, and ARVC phenocopies.

subject: van Tintelen et al. (2009)
object: van Tintelen et al. (2009) identified an identical missense mutation in the head domain of desmin, p.S13F, in 27 carriers or obligate carriers from 5 families with desmin-related myopathy; the mutation was a founder mutation and was fully penetrant.

subject: van Tintelen et al. (2009)
object: van Tintelen et al. (2009) reported that the DES p.S13F mutation shared by 5 families was a founder mutation.

subject: van Tintelen et al. (2009)
object: Because of the clinical overlap with desmosomal cardiomyopathies, van Tintelen et al. (2009) studied intercalated disks in hearts of DES p.S13F carriers and found normal amounts of major desmosomal proteins but more convoluted, elongated intercalated disks with a zigzag appearance. They suggested that a localized effect of desmin on cardiac intercalated disk structure might contribute to pathogenesis.

subject: Otten et al. (2010)
object: Otten et al. (2010) evaluated 2 families carrying different DES mutations. One family was diagnosed with desmin-related myopathy, with an ARVC-like phenotype in 1 patient, whereas the other family presented with severe biventricular cardiomyopathy. The authors concluded that an ARVC-like phenotype or a severe cardiomyopathy with right ventricular involvement are possible, yet infrequent, cardiac phenotypes in desmin-related myopathy.

subject: Otten et al. (2010)
object: Otten et al. (2010) identified a DES missense mutation, p.N342D, in a family with desmin-related myopathy in which 1 patient had an ARVC-like phenotype.

subject: Otten et al. (2010)
object: Otten et al. (2010) identified a DES mutation, p.R454W, in a family with severe biventricular cardiomyopathy. Immunohistochemistry of myocardial tissue from 2 mutation carriers showed desmin aggregates and decreased desmoplakin and plakophilin-2 at the intercalated disk, suggesting a link between desmosomal cardiomyopathies and cardiomyopathies caused by DES mutations.

subject: Otten et al. (2010)
object: Otten et al. (2010) screened the DES gene in 50 patients with ARVC or ARVC-like phenotypes and found no additional DES mutations, indicating that DES mutations are an infrequent cause of ARVC.

subject: van Spaendonck-Zwarts et al. (2011)
object: van Spaendonck-Zwarts et al. (2011) described desmin-related myopathy (DRM) as an autosomally inherited skeletal and cardiac myopathy, mainly caused by dominant mutations in the desmin gene (DES).

subject: van Spaendonck-Zwarts et al. (2011)
object: In a meta-analysis of 159 reported DES mutation carriers with 40 different mutations, van Spaendonck-Zwarts et al. (2011) found neurological signs in 74% and cardiological signs in 74% of carriers; 49% had both, 22% had isolated neurological signs, and 22% had isolated cardiological signs. More than 70% had myopathy or muscular weakness, with normal creatine kinase in one-third of them; up to 50% had cardiomyopathy and around 60% had cardiac conduction disease or arrhythmias, with atrioventricular block as an important hallmark.

subject: van Spaendonck-Zwarts et al. (2011)
object: van Spaendonck-Zwarts et al. (2011) noted that symptoms generally began in the fourth decade; a quarter of carriers died at a mean age of 49 years, and sudden cardiac death occurred in 2 patients with a pacemaker, suggesting ventricular tachyarrhythmia as the cause of death.

subject: van Spaendonck-Zwarts et al. (2011)
object: van Spaendonck-Zwarts et al. (2011) found that most DES mutations were missense mutations, mostly located in the 2B domain. Mutations in the 2B domain predominated in patients with an isolated neurological phenotype, whereas head and tail domain mutations predominated in patients with an isolated cardiological phenotype.

subject: Greenberg et al. (2012)
object: Greenberg et al. (2012) found that limb girdle muscular dystrophy 1D/1E (LGMD1D/1E), a skeletal and cardiac myopathy previously linked to chromosome 6q23, was caused by a splice donor site mutation in the desmin gene (DES) on chromosome 2q35. They found the mutation (IVS3+3A>G) by sequencing a patient and family members.

subject: Greenberg et al. (2012)
object: Greenberg et al. (2012) used laser capture microdissection to isolate cytoplasmic inclusions from the skeletal muscle of a patient with LGMD1D/1E. Mass spectrometry-based proteomics and bioinformatic analysis of these inclusions showed that desmin was their major constituent.

subject: Greenberg et al. (2012)
object: Greenberg et al. (2012) noted that the disorder they studied was named LGMD1D in OMIM nomenclature and LGMD1E by the Human Gene Nomenclature Committee.

subject: Hedberg et al. (2012)
object: In a Swedish family with autosomal dominant myofibrillar myopathy with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC), Hedberg et al. (2012) used exome sequencing to identify a heterozygous c.1255C>T transition in the DES gene on chromosome 2q35, resulting in a pro419-to-ser (P419S) substitution. Sanger sequencing of 17 family members confirmed the mutation in 7 of the 10 family members who had been classified as affected in a previous study.

subject: Hedberg et al. (2012)
object: Hedberg et al. (2012) noted that the Swedish family with myofibrillar myopathy and ARVC had previously shown linkage to chromosome 10q22.3, but no causative mutation had been found in that region; the causative mutation was instead found in the DES gene on chromosome 2q35.

subject: Hedberg et al. (2012)
object: Hedberg et al. (2012) concluded that some dominantly inherited muscle diseases present diagnostic difficulties because they can display wide clinical and morphologic variability even within a single family.

subject: Gudkova et al. (2013)
object: Gudkova et al. (2013) reported what they described as the first case of desmin cardiomyopathy that began in adolescence. Over time the patient's clinical phenotype changed through several types of cardiomyopathy. The authors noted that this made it difficult to diagnose and treat the disease correctly at an early stage.

subject: Gudkova et al. (2013)
object: Gudkova et al. (2013) noted that desmin cardiomyopathy is a rare cause of congestive heart failure. When it appears in adulthood, it is often associated with conduction disorders and a neuromuscular phenotype. The disease can produce a range of clinical phenotypes, including hypertrophic, restrictive, and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

subject: Cetin et al. (2013)
object: Cetin et al. (2013) studied a consanguineous family in which 2 members had autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD2). LGMD2 is marked by progressive weakness of the proximal shoulder and pelvic girdle muscles. Unlike in autosomal dominant desminopathies, skeletal muscle from the patients did not show ultrastructural changes such as disrupted myofibrillar organization, myofibrillar degradation products, or dislocated or aggregated membranous organelles.

subject: Cetin et al. (2013)
object: Cetin et al. (2013) used genome-wide homozygosity mapping in this consanguineous family and mapped the LGMD2 phenotype to chromosome 2q35-q36.3.

subject: Cetin et al. (2013)
object: In the 2 affected members of this consanguineous family, Cetin et al. (2013) sequenced the candidate gene DES and found a homozygous splice-site mutation, c.1289-2A>G. The mutation added 16 amino acids to the desmin tail domain, a region that had been suggested to interact with lamin B.

subject: Cetin et al. (2013)
object: Cetin et al. (2013) found by immunofluorescence and Western blot analysis that the mutant desmin was still expressed and still formed a cytoskeletal network in patient skeletal muscle fibers. Using confocal laser scanning microscopy, they found a specific disruption of the desmin-lamin B interaction in the patient's skeletal muscle. The authors concluded that autosomal recessive DES mutations cause an LGMD2 phenotype without features of myofibrillar myopathy.

subject: Ojrzyńska et al. (2017)
object: Ojrzyńska et al. (2017) reported restrictive cardiomyopathy caused by a novel mutation in the desmin gene.

subject: Straub et al. (2018)
object: Straub et al. (2018) reported on the 229th ENMC international workshop, held in Naarden, the Netherlands, in March 2017, which addressed the nomenclature and a reformed classification of the limb-girdle muscular dystrophies.

subject: Riley et al. (2019)
object: Riley et al. (2019) described 2 sisters who presented in their twenties with slowly progressive limb-girdle weakness, severe systolic dysfunction, and progressive, severe respiratory weakness. Muscle biopsy showed variation in fiber size with more central nuclei. Electron microscopy showed extensive myofibrillar disarray and duplication of the basal lamina, but no inclusions or aggregates.

subject: Riley et al. (2019)
object: In the 2 affected sisters, Riley et al. (2019) identified compound heterozygous variants in the DES gene: a missense variant, p.(Leu190Pro), inherited from the father, and a deep intronic variant in intron 7, inherited from the mother, that was predicted to create a cryptic splice site. The disease segregated with these variants. The father and brothers who carried only the p.(Leu190Pro) variant were clinically unaffected.

subject: DES deep intronic variant within intron-7
Riley et al. (2019)
object: Riley et al. (2019) showed by RNA sequencing and analysis of muscle cDNA that the maternal deep intronic DES variant caused aberrant splicing, inserting an artificial exon/intronic fragment into the transcript. This fragment shifted the reading frame and created a premature termination codon. The resulting nonsense-mediated decay was strong, so that 92% of DES transcripts were paternal and 8% were maternal. Western blot showed a 60 to 75% reduction in desmin, which likely consisted only of the p.(Leu190Pro) mutant desmin.

subject: Riley et al. (2019)
object: Riley et al. (2019) noted that desminopathy is usually autosomal dominant but that a few autosomal recessive cases have been reported. They concluded that their family widened the phenotypic range of recessive DES cardio/myopathy, here without myofibrillar aggregates.
